summary:
Private, adult, consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful in Fiji since 1 February 2010, when the Crimes Decree 2009, cited as the Crimes Act 2010, took effect and repealed the colonial-era Penal Code offence under Article 175, which had carried a maximum penalty of fourteen years' imprisonment. Enforcement had already stopped in practice: in July 2006 Fiji's High Commissioner in New Zealand confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested, two years before repeal.

The 2013 Constitution, Article 26(3)(a), prohibits unfair direct or indirect discrimination on grounds including sex, gender, sexual orientation, and gender identity and expression. The 1997 Constitution had already barred government discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, making Fiji one of the first two countries in the world to do so, alongside South Africa; that constitution was abolished in 2009 and replaced in September 2013. The Asia Pacific Alliance for Sexual and Gender Diversity describes the gender identity and expression clause as unique worldwide.

That constitutional protection has no implementing machinery for trans people. Fiji offers no route to change a gender marker on identity documents, and no legislative or policy framework recognises trans identity, including the traditional third-gender vaka sa lewa lewa (vakasalewalewa), people assigned male at birth who dress, act and behave as female and who have traditionally been accepted in Fijian society. The Asia Pacific Alliance documents resulting marginalisation and discrimination. A trans visitor's documents will not match their presentation, and there is no administrative process to correct that.

Family law provides no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions. The Marriage Act 2002 defines marriage as the union of one man and one woman, an express ban in place since 2002 and reaffirmed by prime ministerial statements on 26 March 2013, in January 2016, and in 2019. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to have that relationship recognised in Fiji.

Conversion therapy is prohibited for registered mental health professionals under the Mental Health Decree 2010, which also provides that a person is not mentally ill by reason of refusing or failing to express a particular sexual orientation. Health professionals are barred from attempting to change sexual orientation.

Blood donation is closed to gay and bisexual men. In April 2017 the Ministry of Health confirmed the ban after a gay man was refused donation on the basis of his sexual orientation.

Violence against LGBTQ people is documented but reported as rare. On 1 July 2001 Red Cross leader John Maurice Scott and his partner Gregory Scrivener were murdered in Suva in an apparent homophobic attack with a possible political motive. A gay student was found dead in Nasinu in September 2017. In May 2018 a young transgender woman was murdered in Suva. Activists describe physical violence and domestic abuse functioning as familial conversion therapy for many LGBTQ+ people.

Reporting is constrained by distrust of police. Accounts of possible police harassment are described as a likely reason LGBTQ people and couples do not report anti-gay violence or hateful discrimination.

Public displays of affection between people of the same sex are not illegal, but are generally considered offensive in Fiji.

Pride organising has been restricted at times and permitted at others. The government has in the past cancelled gay pride marches. Activists held activities on 17 May 2013 for the International Day Against Homophobia and Transphobia, an event in Suva in 2017 drew activists and religious figures, and Fiji's first pride parade took place on 17 May 2018 in Lautoka with a local police escort and an address by former President Epeli Nailatikau.
tangentialFactors:
Fiji's sodomy law was enforced into the 2000s. In April 2005 Australian tourist Thomas McCosker and Fijian man Dhirendra Nadan received two-year prison sentences under Penal Code Article 175 for consensual sex; the trial judge described the acts as so disgusting that any decent person would vomit. Human Rights Watch called for the charges to be dropped and the men released, citing the 1997 constitutional prohibition on sexual orientation discrimination. The convictions were overturned in August 2005 by the highest court as a violation of the Constitution.

Prime Minister Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex days after those sentences, calling homosexuality a sin in what he described as the conservative Christian nation. The New Zealand AIDS Foundation, through executive director Rachael Le Mesurier, linked criminalisation to the undergrounding of sex and the spread of HIV.

Fiji's constitutional protections have been interrupted. The 1997 Constitution, which barred government discrimination on sexual orientation, was abolished in 2009 during the period of emergency rule that ousted the prime minister, and replaced by the September 2013 Constitution.
localsOnly:
Discrimination in employment on the basis of sexual orientation has been banned since 2007 under the Employment Relations Promulgation 2007. In 2013 the government extended sexual orientation and gender identity protections into anti-hate-speech law and into law governing discrimination in certain businesses.

Political representation has advanced unevenly. In 2022 the National Federation Party endorsed Divina Loloma, a transgender woman, as the first openly LGBTQ candidate ever endorsed by a political party in Fiji, while All People's Party leader Tuiloma Tawaivuna criticised the nomination, calling transgender people an abomination and Biblically wrong.

Religious institutions shape the climate. The majority Methodist and Catholic denominations traditionally view transgender identities negatively, and the Muslim minority, about 6 per cent of the population, tends to treat cross-dressing as sinful behaviour that needs to be fixed. Social mores on sexual orientation and gender identity are described as conservative, with little public support for LGBTQ rights, and reports of societal discrimination and bullying are not uncommon.

Advocacy organisations for LGBTQ people are unable to register under Fiji's rules. Intersex bodily autonomy is not protected in law.
outOfScopeNotes:
Outright International's country overview carries a summary flag listing same-sex relations as illegal, which contradicts its own narrative text and the statutory record of decriminalisation in 2010; the discrepancy is unresolved in the source.

Whether the May 2018 killing of a transgender woman in Suva was prosecuted, and whether it was recorded as a hate crime, is not established in the sources. The circumstances of the September 2017 death of a gay student in Nasinu are likewise not established.

Hate-crime reports are described as rare, but the sources do not indicate whether Fiji maintains systematic hate-crime recording, so the absence of reports cannot be read as an absence of incidents.

The GlobalGayz country page is a legacy-era overview whose statement that discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity was not banned predates the 2013 Constitution.
